item.question: Explain why a number times 5 is the number times 10 divided by 2, using 8 × 5.
steps_tex: $8 \times 10$ means $8$ groups of $10$, which is $80$.
$5$ is half of $10$, so each group has half as many.
So $8 \times 5$ is half of $80$, which is $40$.
In general, $5 = 10 \div 2$, so $n \times 5 = (n \times 10) \div 2$.
Dividing first also works: $(8 \div 2) \times 10 = 40$.
item.answer_tex: $5 = 10 \div 2$, so times $5$ is times $10$ then halve, e.g. $8 \times 5 = 40$
steps: 8 × 10 means 8 groups of 10, which is 80.

So 8 × 5 is half of 80, which is 40.
In general, 5 = 10 ÷ 2, so n × 5 = (n × 10) ÷ 2.
Dividing first also works: (8 ÷ 2) × 10 = 40.

item.question: Is Roxie right that two 2-digit numbers give a 3-digit or 4-digit product? Can two 3-digit numbers give a 4-digit product? Can a 4-digit number times a 2-digit number give a 5-digit product?
steps_tex: Smallest: $10 \times 10 = 100$, which has $3$ digits.
Largest: $99 \times 99 = 9801$, which has $4$ digits.
Every other product lies between them, so Roxie is right.
Two $3$-digit numbers: the smallest is $100 \times 100 = 10,000$, which already has $5$ digits. So never $4$ digits.
For a $4$-digit and a $2$-digit number: the smallest is $1000 \times 10 = 10,000$, which has $5$ digits, so yes.
The largest is $9999 \times 99 = 9,89,901$, which has $6$ digits.
item.answer_tex: Roxie is right; two $3$-digit numbers never give $4$ digits; a $4$-digit times a $2$-digit number can give $5$ digits or $6$ digits
steps: Smallest: 10 × 10 = 100, which has 3 digits.
Largest: 99 × 99 = 9801, which has 4 digits.
Every other product lies between them, so Roxie is right.
Two 3-digit numbers: the smallest is 100 × 100 = 10,000, which already has 5 digits. So never 4 digits.
A 4-digit and a 2-digit number: the smallest is 1000 × 10 = 10,000, which has 5 digits, so yes.
The largest is 9999 × 99 = 9,89,901, which has 6 digits.
item.answer: Roxie is right; two 3-digit numbers never give 4 digits; a 4-digit times a 2-digit number can give 5 digits (or 6)
item.text:
$1$. Smallest: $10 \times 10 = 100$, which has $3$ digits.
$2$. Largest: $99 \times 99 = 9801$, which has $4$ digits.
$3$. Every other product lies between them, so Roxie is right.
$4$. Two $3$-digit numbers: the smallest is $100 \times 100 = 10,000$, which already has $5$ digits. So never $4$ digits.
$5$. For a $4$-digit and a $2$-digit number: the smallest is $1000 \times 10 = 10,000$, which has $5$ digits, so yes.
$6$. The largest is $9999 \times 99 = 9,89,901$, which has $6$ digits.
Answer: Roxie is right; two $3$-digit numbers never give $4$ digits; a $4$-digit times a $2$-digit number can give $5$ digits or $6$ digits

steps_tex: For a $1$-digit number times a $1$-digit number the counts are $1$ and $2$: $1 + 1 - 1 = 1$ and $1 + 1 = 2$.
Multiplying a $5$-digit number by a $5$-digit number gives $5 + 5 - 1 = 9$ or $5 + 5 = 10$ digits.

Multiplying a $12$-digit number by a $13$-digit number gives $12 + 13 - 1 = 24$ or $12 + 13 = 25$ digits.
Rule: an $m$-digit number times an $n$-digit number has $m + n - 1$ or $m + n$ digits.
